evidence.excerpt: This study examined how adults with no medical background interpret conditional probability expressions (e.g., '1 in 10 women with a positive result actually has cancer') in cervical screening information leaflets distributed by Serbian public health centres. Thirty-two participants aged 22–58 were recruited from a general-population sample in Novi Sad. Think-aloud protocols were recorded during reading and subsequently coded for interpretation errors, emotional reactions, and decision intentions. Results showed that 68% of participants misread positive predictive value as diagnostic certainty, and 41% expressed intention to avoid further screening after misunderstanding a false-positive rate. Frequency formats ('3 out of every 100') produced significantly fewer errors than percentage formats (p < .01). Qualitative analysis identified four dominant lay mental models of screening accuracy. Findings suggest that current Serbian screening leaflets require substantial revision of probability language and recommend adoption of frequency-based icon arrays as a supplement to text.
